newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT--Commodity index futures rise led by oil.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT--Commodity index futures rise led by oil.

text.p: U.S. commodity index futures pushed up to two-week highs midday Thursday, with the ongoing rally in oil futures offsetting weakness in precious metals and coffee, cocoa, sugar and cotton.

"The two key areas for commodities remain crude oil, heating and the grains, but the recovery in copper in the past two weeks has removed a major drag from the CRB also as it has only copper in its base metal sector weightings," Merrill Lynch senior commodities strategist Bill O'Neill said.
CME October Goldman Sachs Commodity Index (GSCI) futures were up 1.10 points at 205.50 midday, after edging up to a two week high at 206.10 intraday, which was also a contract high.
The GSCI index itself was up 0.02 points at 205.13.
GSCI futures have been steadily recovering in the past two weeks from the lows at 191.00 in early August.
The less active NYFE November CRB futures contract was off 0.10 points at 245.90 midday, from a session high at 246.75, but its recovery from lows of 239.50 in late July continued.
With a 49 percent weighting in the energy sector, GSCI futures were benefitting more than the CRB futures from the rally in crude oil and heating oil, analysts said.

Benchmark NYMEX crude oil futures, which usually provide direction for London's IPE Brent oil futures, have been rising steadily again since mid-summer, driven by low U.S. heating oil and European gasoil supplies ahead of the winter.

NYMEX November crude oil futures climbed to $24.62 a barrel Thursday, testing the November contract's contract high of $24.64 set on September 13, though nearby NYMEX crude has yet to break the five-year highs at $25.70 seen in April this year on the weekly continuation charts.

Back months in NYMEX crude did see life-of-contract highs Thursday though, continuing the rise in the 12 month crude strip, which closed at $21.74 a barrel Wednesday, up from $19.72 in June, though the whole strip remains backwardated.
"Crude oil and product charts have been consistently bullish and pointed to sharply higher levels as far back as early July," O'Neill said.
In addition, the postponement of the U.N./Iraq oil deal earlier this month, after Iraq's incursion into northern Iraq's Kurdish area, has also helped boost oil prices.

"Crude oil remains overweight in our recommendations in a diversified commodity portfolio, with recent American Petroleum Institute (API) reports bullish for heating oil as inventories are at historically low levels," O'Neill said.

NYMEX November heating oil futures, now the most active contract ahead of the expiry of October heating oil on September 30, saw fresh life-of-contract highs at 71.80 cents Thursday, while the nearby but expiring October contract saw five year highs at 72.80 cents on the weekly charts.

The heating oil futures strip remains narrowly backwardated, though the November heating oil/crude crack spread has climbed sharply to $5.58 a barrel intraday Thursday, up from a low of $3.61 a barrel in June.

But the November 3-2-1 crack spread, a proxy for refining margins, remains depressed at $3.19 a barrel Thursday, down from a summer high of $4.30, providing little incentive for increased refinery runs and distillate stocks, analysts said.

"Even if stocks grow by the amount they usually do in September, distillate inventories (which include heating oil) will still begin the last quarter 1995 about 10 to 20 million barrels below the recent average", the API warned recently.
"But the demand for heating oil could actually be lower this winter than last year, if this winter is less severe and closer to the historical norm," the API said.
"Stronger transportation demand (for diesel fuel) and weaker heating demand may offset each other, causing total demand to be roughly the same as last year."
--Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1641
